terms.definition: to get up; to stand up
to shower; to take a shower
to take a bath; to bathe
to comb one's hair; to brush one's hair
to put on makeup; to do one's makeup
to go to bed; to lie down
to be called; to be named
to have fun; to enjoy oneself
to get sick; to become ill
to be glad; to be happy about something
to get bored; to be bored
to get tired; to become tired
to get ready; to prepare oneself
to get together; to meet up
to meet up with; to run into (someone)
reflexive pronoun for él/ella/usted and ellos/ellas/ustedes
dormir = to sleep (general); dormirse = to fall asleep (the moment of falling asleep)
lavar = to wash something; lavarse = to wash oneself
ir = to go (somewhere); irse = to leave; to go away
despertar = to wake someone up; despertarse = to wake up (yourself)

questions.correct: to get up; to stand up
incorrect: to lie down; to go to bed
questions.why_correct: 'Levantarse' contains 'levantar' (to lift/raise) — you lift yourself up. 'Me levanto' = I get up.
why_wrong: 'Dormirse' means to fall asleep — the opposite action from getting up.
'Sentarse' means to sit down — to lower yourself into a seat, not rise from one.
'Acostarse' means to go to bed / lie down — again the opposite, going horizontal.
questions.tip: Think about 'levantar' — to lift or raise. What would you do to yourself when getting out of bed?

questions.q: How do you say 'to get up; to stand up'?
questions.why_correct: 'Levantarse' is from 'levantar' (to lift/raise) + reflexive -se: you raise yourself.
why_wrong: 'Acostarse' means to go to bed; to lie down.
questions.tip: The root verb 'levantar' means to lift or raise — what is the reflexive form?

questions.why_correct: 'Despertarse' (e→ie) comes from 'despertar' (to awaken someone). The reflexive form means you wake yourself up — 'Me despierto a las siete' = I wake up at seven.
why_wrong: 'Dormirse' means to fall asleep — the opposite moment: when you close your eyes, not open them.
'Levantarse' means to get up (physically out of bed) — you can wake up before you get up.
There is no common reflexive verb for 'to yawn'; 'tener sueño' means to be sleepy.
questions.tip: Think of 'el despertador' — that's Spanish for an alarm clock. What does an alarm clock do to you?

questions.q: How do you say 'to wake up'?
questions.why_correct: 'Despertarse' is the reflexive form of 'despertar' (to wake someone). E→ie stem change: yo me despierto.
why_wrong: 'Dormirse' means to fall asleep — opposite of waking up.
'Levantarse' means to get up — the physical act of rising from bed, not the moment of waking.
questions.tip: The noun 'el despertador' (alarm clock) contains this verb. What does the alarm do?

questions.correct: to shower; to take a shower
incorrect: to take a bath; to bathe
questions.why_correct: 'Ducharse' comes from 'la ducha' (shower). 'Me ducho por la mañana' = I shower in the morning.
why_wrong: 'Bañarse' means to take a bath — a tub bath, not a shower. 'El baño' = bathroom/bath.
'Lavarse el pelo' means to wash one's hair — a specific part of hygiene, not the full shower.
'Vestirse' means to get dressed — this happens after bathing, not during.
questions.tip: Think of 'la ducha' — what bathroom fixture is that in English?

questions.q: How do you say 'to shower; to take a shower'?
questions.why_correct: 'Ducharse' is from 'la ducha' (the shower). Regular -ar reflexive verb.
why_wrong: 'Bañarse' means to take a bath in a tub.
'Lavarse' means to wash (oneself) — more general, or used for specific body parts like 'lavarse las manos'.
questions.tip: The noun 'la ducha' means shower — what reflexive verb comes from it?

questions.correct: to take a bath; to bathe
questions.why_correct: 'Bañarse' comes from 'el baño' (the bath/bathroom). In many Latin American countries, 'bañarse' is used more broadly to mean bathing in general (including showering).
why_wrong: 'Ducharse' specifically means to take a shower using a shower head.
'Lavarse la cara' means to wash one's face — a more specific action.
'Nadar' means to swim — though water is involved, 'bañarse' refers to bathing for hygiene, not sport.
questions.tip: Think of 'el baño' — what room in the house does that describe?

questions.q: How do you say 'to take a bath; to bathe'?
questions.why_correct: 'Bañarse' is from 'el baño' (bath/bathroom). Regular -ar reflexive verb.
why_wrong: 'Ducharse' means to take a shower specifically.
'Lavarse' means to wash (oneself) — general washing, not specifically bathing.
'Mojarse' means to get wet — not the same as intentionally bathing.
questions.tip: The noun 'el baño' (bath/bathroom) gives you the verb. What reflexive form does it take?

questions.why_correct: 'Lavarse' = 'lavar' (to wash) + reflexive -se. 'Lavarse las manos' = to wash one's hands. The action of washing applies to oneself.
why_wrong: 'Peinarse' means to comb/brush one's hair — a grooming action, not washing.
'Cepillarse los dientes' means to brush one's teeth.
'Secarse' means to dry off — what you do after washing.
questions.tip: Think of 'lavar' (to wash something). Made reflexive — who receives the action?

questions.q: How do you say 'to wash (oneself); to wash up'?
questions.why_correct: 'Lavarse' = 'lavar' (to wash) made reflexive. 'Me lavo las manos' = I wash my hands.
questions.tip: Think of 'lavar' (to wash). 'Lavarse las manos' means to wash one's ___.

questions.correct: to comb one's hair; to brush one's hair
questions.why_correct: 'Peinarse' comes from 'el peine' (comb). It means grooming your hair with a comb or brush. 'Me peino antes de salir' = I brush my hair before going out.
why_wrong: 'Cepillarse los dientes' means to brush one's teeth — a brush, but on teeth, not hair.
'Maquillarse' means to put on makeup — cosmetics, not hair grooming.
'Afeitarse' means to shave — a razor, not a comb.
questions.tip: Think of 'el peine' — what small grooming tool is that in English?

questions.q: How do you say 'to comb one's hair; to brush one's hair'?
questions.why_correct: 'Peinarse' is from 'el peine' (comb). Regular -ar reflexive verb.
why_wrong: 'Cepillarse los dientes' means to brush one's teeth.
questions.tip: The noun 'el peine' (comb) gives you the verb. What reflexive form does it take?

questions.why_correct: 'Cepillarse' comes from 'el cepillo' (brush). 'Los dientes' = the teeth. Together: to brush one's teeth. 'Me cepillo los dientes dos veces al día' = I brush my teeth twice a day.
why_wrong: 'Peinarse' means to comb/brush one's hair — also uses a brush, but for hair, not teeth.
There is no common reflexive verb for 'to put on lipstick'; it falls under 'maquillarse'.
'Enjuagarse' means to rinse oneself — different from brushing.
questions.tip: 'El cepillo' means brush, 'los dientes' means the teeth — what daily hygiene task do these together describe?

questions.q: How do you say 'to brush one's teeth'?
questions.why_correct: 'Cepillarse los dientes' = 'el cepillo' (brush) + reflexive + 'los dientes' (the teeth).
why_wrong: 'Peinarse' means to comb/brush one's hair, not teeth.
'Lavarse la cara' means to wash one's face.
'Afeitarse' means to shave — also involves the face, but with a razor, not a toothbrush.
questions.tip: You need the reflexive of 'el cepillo' (brush) combined with 'los dientes' (the teeth).

questions.correct: to put on makeup; to do one's makeup
questions.why_correct: 'Maquillarse' comes from 'el maquillaje' (makeup). 'Me maquillo antes de salir' = I put on makeup before going out.
why_wrong: 'Afeitarse' means to shave — also a grooming task but involves a razor, not cosmetics.
'Vestirse' means to get dressed — putting on clothing, not cosmetics.
'Peinarse' means to comb/brush one's hair — hair grooming, not makeup.
questions.tip: Think of 'el maquillaje' — what beauty product is that in English?

questions.q: How do you say 'to put on makeup; to do one's makeup'?
questions.why_correct: 'Maquillarse' is from 'el maquillaje' (makeup). Regular -ar reflexive verb.
why_wrong: 'Ponerse' means to put on clothing — not makeup specifically.
questions.tip: The noun 'el maquillaje' (makeup) gives you the verb.

questions.why_correct: 'Afeitarse' comes from 'la afeitadora' (razor/electric shaver) or 'afeitar' (to shave someone). The reflexive means you shave yourself. 'Mi padre se afeita cada mañana' = My father shaves every morning.
why_wrong: 'Cepillarse los dientes' means to brush one's teeth — a brush to the face area, but a very different action.
'Peinarse' means to comb/brush hair — grooming hair, not removing facial hair.
There is no common reflexive verb specifically for 'deodorant'; 'ponerse desodorante' would be used.
questions.tip: Think of 'la afeitadora' — what grooming appliance is that?

questions.q: How do you say 'to shave; to shave oneself'?
questions.why_correct: 'Afeitarse' is from 'la afeitadora' (razor). Regular -ar reflexive verb.
why_wrong: 'Cepillarse los dientes' means to brush one's teeth.
'Maquillarse' means to put on makeup — applying something to the face, but cosmetics, not a razor.
questions.tip: The noun 'la afeitadora' (razor/shaver) gives you the verb.

questions.why_correct: 'Vestirse' (e→i) comes from 'vestir' (to dress someone). The reflexive means to dress yourself. 'Me visto rápidamente' = I get dressed quickly. Note: e→i stem change in all forms except nosotros/vosotros.
why_wrong: 'Ponerse' means to put on a single garment (a coat, shoes, etc.) — more specific than the full act of getting dressed.
'Quitarse' means to take off clothing — the opposite of vestirse.
'Probarse' means to try on clothing — in a fitting room, not getting dressed for the day.
questions.tip: Think of 'vestir' (to dress someone else). Made reflexive — who gets dressed now?

questions.q: How do you say 'to get dressed'?
questions.why_correct: 'Vestirse' (e→i) is the full act of getting dressed. Conjugation: me visto, te vistes, se viste, nos vestimos.
why_wrong: 'Ponerse' means to put on a specific item of clothing.
'Quitarse' means to take off clothing — the opposite.
'Probarse' means to try on clothing in a store.
questions.tip: The non-reflexive 'vestir' means to dress someone else. Add the reflexive — who does the dressing now?

questions.why_correct: 'Ponerse' = 'poner' (to put/place) + reflexive. 'Me pongo el abrigo' = I put on my coat. It refers to the act of putting on a specific garment.
why_wrong: 'Vestirse' means to get dressed completely — the full morning routine of getting dressed, not a single item.
'Quitarse' means to take off clothing — the opposite action.
'Llevar' means to wear or to be wearing (a state, not an action).
questions.tip: Think of 'poner' (to put or place). Made reflexive with 'la ropa' (clothing).

questions.q: How do you say 'to put on (clothing)'?
questions.why_correct: 'Ponerse' = reflexive of 'poner' (to put). 'Me pongo los zapatos' = I put on my shoes.
why_wrong: 'Llevar' means to wear (a state) — 'Llevo una camisa roja' = I'm wearing a red shirt.
questions.tip: The root verb 'poner' means to put or place. Made reflexive — what do you put on yourself?

questions.why_correct: 'Quitarse' = 'quitar' (to remove/take away) + reflexive. 'Me quito los zapatos al llegar a casa' = I take off my shoes when I get home.
why_wrong: 'Ponerse' means to put on clothing — the opposite action.
'Desvestirse' or 'desnudarse' means to get completely undressed — quitarse refers to specific items.
No common reflexive verb means 'to lose clothing'; 'perder' (to lose) is non-reflexive here.
questions.tip: Think of 'quitar' (to remove or take away). Made reflexive with 'la ropa'.

questions.q: How do you say 'to take off (clothing)'?
questions.why_correct: 'Quitarse' = 'quitar' (to remove) + reflexive. 'Me quito la chaqueta' = I take off my jacket.
why_wrong: 'Ponerse' means to put on — the opposite.
'Desvestirse' means to completely undress — broader than taking off a single item.
questions.tip: The root verb 'quitar' means to remove. Made reflexive — what do you remove from yourself?

questions.correct: to go to bed; to lie down
questions.why_correct: 'Acostarse' (o→ue) comes from 'acostar' (to put someone to bed). 'Me acuesto a las diez' = I go to bed at ten. Note the stem change: me acuesto, te acuestas, se acuesta.
why_wrong: 'Dormirse' means to fall asleep — what happens after you go to bed, not the act of going.
'Despertarse' means to wake up — the opposite end of the sleeping cycle.
'Levantarse' means to get up — the morning action, opposite of going to bed.
questions.tip: Think of 'acostar' (to put someone to bed). Made reflexive — what do you do to yourself at night?

questions.q: How do you say 'to go to bed; to lie down'?
questions.why_correct: 'Acostarse' (o→ue) = 'acostar' (to put to bed) made reflexive. Me acuesto, te acuestas, se acuesta.
why_wrong: 'Dormirse' means to fall asleep — different from the act of going to bed.
'Levantarse' means to get up — opposite action.
questions.tip: The root verb 'acostar' means to put someone to bed. Made reflexive, with o→ue stem change.

questions.why_correct: 'Dormirse' (o→ue) = 'dormir' (to sleep) made reflexive. The reflexive emphasizes the moment of falling asleep. 'Me dormí en el sofá' = I fell asleep on the couch.
why_wrong: 'Dormir' (non-reflexive) means to sleep — the ongoing state of sleeping, not the moment of falling asleep.
'Acostarse' means to go to bed — the physical act of getting into bed, which happens before you fall asleep.
'Dormir una siesta' means to take a nap — a type of sleeping, but still 'dormir', not 'dormirse'.
questions.tip: Compare 'dormir' (to sleep) to its reflexive form. One captures a specific moment — which one?

questions.q: How do you say 'to fall asleep'?
questions.why_correct: 'Dormirse' (o→ue) is the reflexive of 'dormir'. It captures the moment of falling asleep. Me duermo, te duermes, se duerme.
why_wrong: 'Dormir' means to sleep (the ongoing state) — not the specific moment of falling asleep.
'Acostarse' means to go to bed — different from actually falling asleep.
'Descansar' means to rest — not necessarily to fall asleep.
questions.tip: You need the reflexive of 'dormir'. Think: ongoing state of sleeping vs. the moment you fall asleep.

questions.why_correct: 'Sentarse' (e→ie) = 'sentar' (to seat someone) made reflexive. 'Siéntate aquí' = Sit down here. Stem change: me siento, te sientas, se sienta.
why_wrong: 'Levantarse' means to stand up / get up — the opposite action.
'Ponerse de pie' means to stand up — again the opposite.
There is no common reflexive verb for 'to kneel'; 'arrodillarse' means to kneel.
questions.tip: Think of 'sentar' (to seat someone). Made reflexive — what do you do to yourself?

questions.q: How do you say 'to sit down'?
questions.why_correct: 'Sentarse' (e→ie): me siento, te sientas, se sienta. From 'sentar' (to seat).
why_wrong: 'Levantarse' means to stand up / get up.
'Ponerse de pie' means to stand up (literally: to put oneself on foot).
'Agacharse' means to crouch down / bend over — not to sit.
questions.tip: The root verb 'sentar' means to seat someone. Made reflexive with e→ie stem change.

questions.correct: to be called; to be named
questions.why_correct: 'Llamarse' = 'llamar' (to call) made reflexive — you are called by a name. '¿Cómo te llamas?' = What is your name? (lit. What do you call yourself?)
why_wrong: 'Llamar' (non-reflexive) means to call someone else — 'Te llamo esta noche' = I'll call you tonight.
'Ser famoso' means to be famous — not related to one's name.
'Presentarse' means to introduce oneself — different from simply being named.
questions.tip: Think of the question '¿Cómo te llamas?' — the most familiar use of this verb.

questions.q: How do you say 'to be called; to be named'?
questions.why_correct: 'Llamarse' = reflexive of 'llamar'. 'Me llamo Ana' = My name is Ana (I am called Ana).
why_wrong: 'Llamar' means to call someone else — non-reflexive.
'Presentarse' means to introduce oneself — more formal, not just stating your name.
'Nombrarse' is not commonly used for personal names in everyday Spanish.
questions.tip: You use this verb every time you ask someone's name: '¿Cómo te ___?'

questions.correct: to have fun; to enjoy oneself
questions.why_correct: 'Divertirse' (e→ie) = 'divertir' (to amuse/entertain someone) made reflexive. You amuse yourself. '¡Diviértete!' = Have fun! Stem change: me divierto, te diviertes, se divierte.
why_wrong: 'Divertir' (non-reflexive) means to amuse or entertain someone else.
'Practicar deportes' means to play sports — an activity that might be fun, but not the same verb.
'Reírse' means to laugh — a possible result of having fun, but a different verb.
questions.tip: Think of 'divertir' (to amuse someone else). Made reflexive — you amuse yourself.

questions.q: How do you say 'to have fun; to enjoy oneself'?
questions.why_correct: 'Divertirse' (e→ie): me divierto, te diviertes, se divierte, nos divertimos.
why_wrong: 'Divertir' means to entertain or amuse someone else.
'Jugar' means to play — a possible activity, but not 'to have fun' specifically.
'Reírse' means to laugh — a reaction, not the general concept of having fun.
questions.tip: The root verb 'divertir' means to entertain someone. Made reflexive with e→ie stem change.

questions.why_correct: 'Sentirse' (e→ie) refers to emotional or physical feelings about oneself. 'Me siento cansada' = I feel tired. 'Me siento bien' = I feel well. Note: e→ie stem change.
why_wrong: 'Sentarse' (e→ie) means to sit down — completely different verb despite similar spelling. 'Sentarse' vs 'sentirse' is a common mix-up.
'Sentir' (non-reflexive) can mean to sense/perceive something external or to feel sorry ('Lo siento' = I'm sorry).
'Doler' means to hurt/ache — 'Me duele la cabeza' = My head hurts. Different construction.
questions.tip: Watch out — 'sentirse' and 'sentarse' look very similar. This one is about your internal state, not your position.

questions.q: How do you say 'to feel (a certain way)'?
questions.why_correct: 'Sentirse' (e→ie) = 'sentir' made reflexive. Used for how you feel. Me siento, te sientes, se siente.
why_wrong: 'Sentarse' means to sit down — easy to confuse with 'sentirse' but completely different.
'Sentir' means to feel/sense something external, or to feel sorry.
'Estar' is used with adjectives to describe states ('Estoy cansado'), but 'sentirse' is specifically 'to feel'.
questions.tip: Don't confuse this with 'sentarse' (to sit down). This verb describes how you feel inside.

questions.correct: to get sick; to become ill
questions.why_correct: 'Enfermarse' = 'enfermar' (to get sick) + reflexive. 'El/la enfermo/a' = sick person. 'Me enfermé la semana pasada' = I got sick last week.
why_wrong: 'Cansarse' means to get tired — uncomfortable, but not the same as becoming ill.
'Dolerle la cabeza' means to have a headache — a symptom, not the general concept of getting sick.
'Tomar medicina' / 'medicarse' means to take medicine — a response to being sick, not getting sick.
questions.tip: Think of 'el enfermo' or 'la enferma' — the Spanish word for a sick person.

questions.q: How do you say 'to get sick; to become ill'?
questions.why_correct: 'Enfermarse' is from 'el/la enfermo/a' (sick person). Regular -ar reflexive verb.
why_wrong: 'Cansarse' means to get tired — not the same as getting sick.
'Doler' means to hurt/ache — a symptom, not the process of falling ill.
'Recuperarse' means to recover — what happens after you get sick.
questions.tip: The adjective 'enfermo/a' (sick) gives you the root. What reflexive verb comes from it?

questions.why_correct: 'Quedarse' = 'quedar' + reflexive. Emphasizes staying in one place. 'Me quedo en casa hoy' = I'm staying home today. 'Quédate aquí' = Stay here.
why_wrong: 'Irse' means to leave / go away — the opposite of staying.
'Esperar' means to wait — you might stay and wait, but they're different concepts.
questions.tip: Think of the command '¡Quédate aquí!' — what are you being told to do?

questions.q: How do you say 'to stay; to remain'?
questions.why_correct: 'Quedarse' is the reflexive of 'quedar'. 'Me quedo' = I stay.
why_wrong: 'Irse' means to leave — opposite of staying.
'Esperar' means to wait — not the same as staying.
'Volver' means to return — implies you left and came back.
questions.tip: The root verb 'quedar' made reflexive. Think of '¡Quédate!' — what does it mean?

questions.why_correct: 'Irse' = 'ir' (to go) made reflexive. The reflexive adds the nuance of departing from the current location. '¡Vámonos!' = Let's get out of here! / Let's go! 'Se fue' = He/she left.
why_wrong: 'Ir' (non-reflexive) means to go to a specific destination — 'Voy al colegio' = I go to school. 'Irse' emphasizes leaving, not a specific destination.
'Escaparse' / 'huir' means to run away/flee — implies urgency or escape, not just leaving.
'Desaparecer' means to disappear — not the same as leaving.
questions.tip: Compare 'ir' (to go to a specific place) to its reflexive form. The reflexive adds the idea of departing.

questions.q: How do you say 'to leave; to go away'?
questions.why_correct: 'Irse' = reflexive of 'ir'. 'Me voy' = I'm leaving. Conjugated like 'ir' but with reflexive pronouns.
why_wrong: 'Ir' means to go to somewhere specific, not to leave.
'Salir' means to go out / to exit — often used for leaving a place, but more literal than 'irse'.
'Marcharse' is a near-synonym of 'irse' (to leave/depart) — both are acceptable, but 'irse' is more common.
questions.tip: Compare 'ir' (to go somewhere) to its reflexive. Think: leaving where you are vs. going to a new place.

questions.why_correct: 'Preocuparse' = 'preocupar' (to worry someone) made reflexive. 'No te preocupes' = Don't worry. 'Me preocupa mucho' uses non-reflexive; 'Me preocupo' uses reflexive.
why_wrong: 'Cuidar' means to take care of someone — 'cuidar a alguien' — different word and concept.
'Tener cuidado' means to be careful — an entirely different phrase.
'Estresarse' means to get/be stressed — close in meaning but 'preocuparse' specifically means to worry.
questions.tip: Think of 'No te preocupes' — the most common Spanish phrase using this verb.

questions.q: How do you say 'to worry; to be worried'?
questions.why_correct: 'Preocuparse' = 'preocupar' made reflexive. 'No te preocupes' = Don't worry.
why_wrong: 'Tener miedo' means to be afraid — fear, not worry.
'Estresarse' means to get stressed — related but different from worrying.
questions.tip: The phrase 'No te ___es' tells someone not to worry. What is the verb?

questions.why_correct: 'Olvidarse' (de) = 'olvidar' (to forget) made reflexive. 'Se me olvidó' = I forgot (it slipped my mind). 'No te olvides de llamarme' = Don't forget to call me.
why_wrong: 'Recordar' means to remember — the opposite of forgetting.
'Perder' means to lose something physically — not the same as forgetting.
'Ignorar' means to ignore — you actively choose to ignore, whereas forgetting is unintentional.
questions.tip: Think of 'olvidar' (to forget something). Made reflexive with 'de'.

questions.why_correct: 'Olvidarse' (de) = reflexive of 'olvidar'. 'Me olvidé de tus llaves' = I forgot your keys.
why_wrong: 'Ignorar' means to ignore — intentional, not forgetful.
questions.tip: The root verb 'olvidar' means to forget. Made reflexive: 'olvidarse de algo'.

questions.correct: to be glad; to be happy about something
questions.why_correct: 'Alegrarse' = 'alegrar' (to make happy) made reflexive. 'Me alegro de verte' = I'm glad to see you. '¡Qué alegría!' = What joy!
why_wrong: 'Entristecerse' / 'ponerse triste' means to become sad — the opposite of alegrarse.
'Reírse' means to laugh; 'divertirse' means to have fun — related to happiness but different verbs.
'Aliviarse' means to feel relieved — a specific type of good feeling, not the same as gladness.
questions.tip: Think of the adjective 'alegre' (happy/cheerful). What reflexive verb comes from it?

questions.q: How do you say 'to be glad; to be happy about something'?
questions.why_correct: 'Alegrarse' = reflexive of 'alegrar'. From 'alegre' (happy/joyful). 'Me alegro mucho' = I'm very glad.
why_wrong: 'Divertirse' means to have fun — fun and gladness are related but distinct.
questions.tip: The adjective 'alegre' (joyful) gives you the verb. 'Me alegro de verte' — what does that suggest?

questions.correct: to get bored; to be bored
questions.why_correct: 'Aburrirse' = 'aburrir' (to bore someone) made reflexive. 'Me aburro en esa clase' = I get bored in that class. 'Estoy aburrido/a' = I'm bored.
why_wrong: 'Aburrir' (non-reflexive) means to bore someone else — 'Esa película me aburre' = That movie bores me.
'Cansarse' means to get tired — physically or mentally exhausted, not necessarily bored.
'Molestarse' / 'enfadarse' means to get annoyed/upset — stronger negative feeling than boredom.
questions.tip: Think of 'aburrir' (to bore someone). Made reflexive — you are now the one experiencing boredom.

questions.q: How do you say 'to get bored; to be bored'?
questions.why_correct: 'Aburrirse' = reflexive of 'aburrir'. 'Me aburro fácilmente' = I get bored easily.
questions.tip: The root verb 'aburrir' means to bore someone. Made reflexive — the feeling now happens to you.

questions.correct: to get tired; to become tired
questions.why_correct: 'Cansarse' = 'cansar' (to tire someone) made reflexive. 'Me canso mucho en el gimnasio' = I get very tired at the gym. 'Estoy cansado/a' = I'm tired.
why_wrong: 'Dormirse' means to fall asleep — what might happen after you get tired, but different moment.
'Aburrirse' means to get bored — mental fatigue, not physical tiredness.
'Enfermarse' means to get sick — a different physical state.
questions.tip: Think of 'el cansancio' (tiredness/fatigue). What reflexive verb comes from 'cansar'?

questions.q: How do you say 'to get tired; to become tired'?
questions.why_correct: 'Cansarse' = reflexive of 'cansar'. From 'el cansancio' (tiredness/fatigue).
questions.tip: The noun 'el cansancio' (fatigue) gives you the root. What reflexive verb does 'cansar' become?

questions.correct: to get ready; to prepare oneself
questions.why_correct: 'Prepararse' = 'preparar' (to prepare something) made reflexive. It means to prepare yourself (shower, get dressed, do hair, etc.) for going out. 'Me preparo en 20 minutos' = I get ready in 20 minutes.
why_wrong: 'Preparar' (non-reflexive) means to prepare something else — 'Preparo el desayuno' = I prepare breakfast.
'Vestirse' is just one part of getting ready (clothing only) — 'prepararse' is the complete process.
'Hacer la maleta' means to pack a suitcase — a preparation, but a specific type.
questions.tip: Think of 'preparar' (to prepare something else). Made reflexive — who is being prepared?

questions.q: How do you say 'to get ready; to prepare oneself'?
questions.why_correct: 'Prepararse' = reflexive of 'preparar'. 'Me preparo rápido' = I get ready fast.
why_wrong: 'Preparar' means to prepare something — food, a lesson, etc.
'Arreglarse' means to get ready / fix oneself up — a near-synonym, but 'prepararse' is more common in daily routine contexts.
questions.tip: The root verb 'preparar' means to prepare something. Made reflexive — who is the subject and object?

questions.correct: to get together; to meet up
incorrect: to run into someone by chance
questions.why_correct: 'Reunirse' = 'reunir' (to gather/unite) made reflexive. Implies a planned meeting. 'Nos reunimos los viernes' = We get together on Fridays. 'La reunión' = the meeting.
why_wrong: 'Encontrarse con' means to run into someone or to meet up — can be planned or unplanned. 'Reunirse' is always a gathering.
'Unirse a' means to join a group/club — different context.
'Casarse' means to get married — not related.
questions.tip: Think of 'la reunión' — what type of gathering or event is that in English?

questions.q: How do you say 'to get together; to meet up'?
questions.why_correct: 'Reunirse' is from 'la reunión' (meeting/gathering). 'Nos reunimos en el parque' = We meet up at the park.
why_wrong: 'Encontrarse con' means to meet up with / run into someone — often one-on-one rather than a group gathering.
'Juntarse' means to get together (near-synonym) — both are acceptable, but 'reunirse' is more formal.
questions.tip: The noun 'la reunión' (meeting/gathering) gives you the verb.

questions.why_correct: 'Darse prisa' = reflexive of 'dar' + 'prisa' (hurry/haste). It describes the act of hurrying. '¡Date prisa!' = Hurry up!
why_wrong: 'Tener prisa' means to be in a hurry (a state) — 'Tengo prisa' = I'm in a hurry. 'Darse prisa' is the action of hurrying.
'Correr' means to run — physical running, though you might run when you hurry.
'Llegar a tiempo' means to arrive on time — the goal, not the action of hurrying.
questions.tip: Think of '¡Date prisa!' — a common command. 'La prisa' means haste.

questions.q: How do you say 'to hurry; to rush'?
questions.why_correct: 'Darse prisa' = reflexive 'darse' + 'prisa' (haste). '¡Daos prisa!' = Hurry up (all of you)!
why_wrong: 'Tener prisa' means to be in a hurry (state) — 'Tengo prisa' = I'm in a hurry.
'Apresurarse' is a synonym — also means to hurry, but 'darse prisa' is the more common phrase.
questions.tip: The phrase literally means 'to give yourself haste'. 'La prisa' = haste or hurry.

questions.correct: to meet up with; to run into (someone)
questions.why_correct: 'Encontrarse con' = 'encontrar' (to find) made reflexive + 'con' (with). When used with people, it means to meet up with or bump into someone. 'Me encontré con Ana en el supermercado' = I ran into Ana at the supermarket.
why_wrong: 'Encontrar' (non-reflexive) means to find an object — 'Encontré mis llaves' = I found my keys.
'Reunirse' means to get together as a group — more planned and group-oriented than 'encontrarse'.
'Descubrir' means to discover something new — different from meeting a person.
questions.tip: Think of 'encontrar' (to find an object). Made reflexive + 'con' — what happens when you 'find' a person?

questions.q: How do you say 'to meet up with; to run into (someone)'?
questions.why_correct: 'Encontrarse con' = reflexive of 'encontrar' + 'con'. 'Nos encontramos en el café' = We met up at the café.
why_wrong: 'Reunirse' means to get together as a group — more formal/planned than running into someone.
'Verse' means to see each other — close in meaning but 'encontrarse' emphasizes the meeting point.
questions.tip: Compare 'encontrar' (to find an object) to its reflexive form used with 'con'.

questions.q: Which reflexive pronoun matches the subject 'yo'?
questions.why_correct: The reflexive pronouns follow subject pronouns: yo → me, tú → te, él/ella → se, nosotros → nos. 'Me levanto' = I get (myself) up.
why_wrong: 'Te' is the reflexive pronoun for 'tú' (you informal).
'Se' is the reflexive pronoun for él/ella/usted and ellos/ellas/ustedes.
questions.tip: There are 5 reflexive pronouns: me, te, se, nos, os — one for each subject pronoun.

questions.why_correct: The reflexive pronoun for 'nosotros' is 'nos'. 'Nos levantamos temprano' = We get up early.
questions.tip: The word 'nosotros' contains a clue about its own reflexive pronoun.

questions.q: How do you say 'I get up' using 'levantarse'?
questions.why_correct: Reflexive pronoun 'me' goes directly before the conjugated verb: me + levanto (yo form of levantar). The pronoun is NEVER placed after a conjugated verb.
why_wrong: 'Levanto me' is wrong — the reflexive pronoun always comes before the conjugated verb in simple tenses.
'Se levanto' uses the wrong pronoun ('se' is for él/ella) and the wrong past tense.
'Me levanta' uses the él/ella form — not the yo form.
questions.tip: The reflexive pronoun always goes directly before the conjugated verb. Which pronoun is for 'yo'?

questions.q: How do you say 'She gets dressed' using 'vestirse' (e→i)?
questions.why_correct: 'Vestirse' is e→i stem-changing and -IR. Ella form: se + viste (stem changes from vest- to vist-). Drop -ir, apply stem change: viste.
why_wrong: 'Se vestise' is not a valid conjugation — the stem must change.
'Te viste' uses the 'tú' reflexive pronoun — correct for 'you get dressed', not 'she'.
'Se vesta' applies an -AR ending (-a) to an -IR verb — wrong verb type ending.
questions.tip: 'Ella' uses 'se'. Apply the e→i stem change to 'vestir'. What is the ella ending for -ir verbs?

questions.q: How do you say 'I go to bed' using 'acostarse' (o→ue)?
questions.why_correct: 'Acostarse' has an o→ue stem change. Yo form: me + acuesto (o→ue). The stem 'acost-' becomes 'acuest-' in all stressed forms except nosotros/vosotros.
why_wrong: 'Me acosto' forgets the stem change — 'acost-' must become 'acuest-' in the yo form.
'Me acuesa' applies an -AR ending incorrectly — it should be '-o' for yo, not '-a'.
'Nos acostamos' is the 'nosotros' form — correct conjugation but wrong subject (we, not I).
questions.tip: Apply o→ue to 'acost-'. The yo form ends in -o. Don't forget the reflexive pronoun for 'yo'.

questions.q: How do you say 'I fall asleep' using 'dormirse' (o→ue)?
questions.why_correct: 'Dormirse' has o→ue stem change. Yo form: me + duermo. The yo form always ends in -o; the stem 'dorm-' becomes 'duerm-'.
why_wrong: 'Me dormo' forgets the stem change — must be 'duerm-' not 'dorm-' in the yo form.
'Se duermo' uses the wrong reflexive pronoun — 'se' is for él/ella, not yo.
'Me duermeo' adds a non-existent extra vowel — the yo ending is simply '-o'.
questions.tip: Apply o→ue to 'dorm-'. The yo form ends in -o. Which reflexive pronoun goes with 'yo'?

questions.why_correct: Tú reflexive pronoun = 'te'. Tú conjugation of -ar verb 'duchar': -as ending. Te + duchas.
why_wrong: 'Me duchas' uses the yo reflexive pronoun 'me' with the tú verb form — mismatched.
'Te ducha' uses the él/ella ending (-a) — wrong for tú.
'Te duchás' uses an Argentine voseo accent mark — not standard Spanish.
questions.tip: The tú reflexive pronoun is 'te'. The tú ending for -ar verbs is '-as'. Apply to 'duchar'.

questions.q: How do you say 'They (ellos) have fun' using 'divertirse' (e→ie)?
questions.why_correct: Ellos reflexive pronoun = 'se'. Ellos form of 'divertirse' (e→ie): se + divierten (stem 'divert-' → 'diviert-').
why_wrong: 'Se diverten' forgets the stem change — must be 'divierten' not 'diverten'.
'Se divertimos' uses the nosotros ending (-imos) with the ellos pronoun — wrong combination.
'Nos divertimos' is correct for 'we have fun', not 'they have fun'.
questions.tip: Ellos uses 'se'. Apply e→ie to 'divert-'. The ellos -ir ending is '-en'.

questions.q: Where does the reflexive pronoun go in a sentence with one conjugated verb?
incorrect: At the end of the sentence
Attached to the end of the conjugated verb
questions.why_correct: In simple tenses with a single conjugated verb, the reflexive pronoun always goes directly before it: 'Me levanto', 'Te duchas', 'Se viste'. It is never split from the verb by other words.
why_wrong: The pronoun never goes after the conjugated verb in simple tenses — 'Levanto me' is wrong.
The pronoun never goes at the end of the sentence.
Attaching to the end works only with infinitives and gerunds — 'levantarse', 'levantándome' — not with conjugated verbs.
questions.tip: Look at any example: 'Me levanto', 'Te duchas', 'Se viste' — where exactly is the reflexive pronoun?

questions.q: In 'Voy a ducharme', where is the reflexive pronoun?
questions.correct: Attached to the end of the infinitive
questions.why_correct: With a conjugated verb + infinitive, the pronoun can attach to the end of the infinitive: 'Voy a ducharme'. Alternatively, it can go before the conjugated verb: 'Me voy a duchar'. Both are correct.
why_wrong: 'Me voy a duchar' is also correct — so 'before the conjugated verb' works too, but this question shows the infinitive-attachment form.
'Voy me a duchar' is wrong — the pronoun cannot go between the conjugated verb and 'a'.
'Voy a me duchar' is wrong — the pronoun cannot go between 'a' and the infinitive without attaching.
questions.tip: Look carefully at 'ducharme' — the pronoun is attached to one specific part of the verb form.

questions.q: What is the difference between 'dormir' and 'dormirse'?
questions.correct: 'Dormir' = to sleep (ongoing state); 'dormirse' = to fall asleep (the moment of falling asleep)
incorrect: 'Dormir' = to sleep a lot; 'dormirse' = to sleep a little
'Dormir' = to sleep at night; 'dormirse' = to nap during the day
'Dormir' and 'dormirse' mean the same thing — the -se is optional
questions.why_correct: The reflexive -se changes the meaning. 'Duermo ocho horas' = I sleep eight hours (ongoing). 'Me dormí en el sofá' = I fell asleep on the couch (the moment it happened). This is the classic non-reflexive/reflexive pair.
why_wrong: The distinction is not about duration or quantity — it's about the moment of falling asleep vs. the state of sleeping.
The distinction is not about time of day — both can occur at any time.
The -se is not optional and does change the meaning — 'dormir' ≠ 'dormirse'.
questions.tip: One form describes the ongoing state of sleeping; the other captures the exact moment of drifting off.

questions.q: What is the difference between 'lavar' and 'lavarse'?
questions.correct: 'Lavar' = to wash something; 'lavarse' = to wash oneself
incorrect: 'Lavar' = to wash in cold water; 'lavarse' = to wash in hot water
'Lavar' = to wash by hand; 'lavarse' = to wash in a machine
'Lavar' and 'lavarse' are the same — -se just sounds more polite
questions.why_correct: Adding -se makes the action reflexive — you wash yourself instead of something else. 'Lavo los platos' = I wash the dishes. 'Me lavo las manos' = I wash my hands (i.e., wash myself).
why_wrong: Temperature has nothing to do with reflexive vs. non-reflexive.
Method of washing has nothing to do with it.
The -se is not a politeness marker — it fundamentally changes who receives the action.
questions.tip: With 'lavar', what is the object? With 'lavarse', who receives the action?

questions.correct: What is your name? (lit. What do you call yourself?)
questions.why_correct: '¿Cómo te llamas?' literally means 'How do you call yourself?' — the reflexive 'llamarse' is used to state one's name. The standard response is 'Me llamo [name]' = My name is [name].
why_wrong: '¿Cómo te sientes?' means 'How do you feel?'
'¿Qué estás haciendo?' means 'What are you doing?'
'¿A quién llamas?' means 'Who are you calling?' — this uses non-reflexive 'llamar'.
questions.tip: The verb 'llamarse' is used here — the reflexive of 'llamar'. '¿Cómo te ___?' = 'How do you ___ yourself?'

questions.correct: My name is Ana (lit. I call myself Ana)
questions.why_correct: 'Me llamo' = reflexive first person of 'llamarse'. Literally 'I call myself' — used to state your name. This is the standard way to introduce yourself in Spanish.
why_wrong: 'Llamé a Ana' means 'I called Ana' — past tense, non-reflexive.
'Ana me llama' means 'Ana is calling me' — non-reflexive, different subject.
'Voy a llamar a Ana' means 'I'm going to call Ana' — non-reflexive, different subject.
questions.tip: 'Me llamo' literally means 'I call myself ___'. Think about what the reflexive of 'llamar' conveys.

questions.q: Nosotros form of 'levantarse' — which is correct?
questions.why_correct: Nosotros: reflexive pronoun 'nos' + levantamos (nosotros -AR ending: -amos). No stem change for nosotros. 'Nos levantamos a las siete' = We get up at seven.
why_wrong: 'Se levantamos' uses the wrong pronoun — 'se' is for él/ella/ellos, not nosotros.
'Nos levantemos' is the subjunctive form — present indicative uses -amos.
'Nos levantan' uses the ellos -AR ending (-an) — wrong for nosotros.
questions.tip: The nosotros reflexive pronoun is 'nos'. The nosotros -ar ending is '-amos'. Nosotros has no stem change.

questions.q: Which reflexive pronoun goes with 'ellos / ellas / ustedes'?
questions.why_correct: Both the él/ella and ellos/ellas forms use 'se' as the reflexive pronoun. 'Se levantan' = they get up. Note: 'se' is used for singular and plural third person.
why_wrong: 'Les' is an indirect object pronoun — not the reflexive pronoun. Don't confuse reflexive and indirect object pronouns.
questions.tip: The same reflexive pronoun is shared by singular and plural third person (él/ella AND ellos/ellas).

questions.q: What does '¿A qué hora te acuestas?' mean?
questions.correct: What time do you go to bed?
incorrect: What time do you wake up?
What time do you fall asleep?
What time do you get up?
questions.why_correct: 'Acostarse' = to go to bed. 'Te acuestas' = you go to bed (tú, with o→ue stem change). '¿A qué hora?' = At what time?
why_wrong: '¿A qué hora te despiertas?' means 'What time do you wake up?' — 'despertarse', not 'acostarse'.
'¿A qué hora te duermes?' means 'What time do you fall asleep?' — 'dormirse', which is after 'acostarse'.
'¿A qué hora te levantas?' means 'What time do you get up?' — 'levantarse', the morning action.
questions.tip: 'Acostarse' means to go to bed. 'Te acuestas' is the tú form. '¿A qué hora?' = At what time?

questions.q: How do you say 'I feel tired' using 'sentirse' (e→ie)?
questions.why_correct: 'Sentirse' (e→ie): yo form = me siento (stem 'sent-' → 'sient-'). 'Cansado/a' agrees with the speaker's gender.
why_wrong: 'Me sento' forgets the stem change — must be 'sient-' not 'sent-' in the yo form.
'Me sienta' uses the él/ella ending (-a) — wrong for yo; also 'sienta' could be confused with 'sentarse' (to sit down).
'Me sentío' uses a false past tense form — not a standard Spanish conjugation.
questions.tip: Apply e→ie to 'sent-'. The yo form ends in -o. The adjective 'cansado/a' describes the feeling.

questions.q: What is the yo form of 'vestirse' (e→i)?
questions.why_correct: 'Vestirse' is e→i (-IR verb). Yo: me + visto (stem 'vest-' → 'vist-'). The 'e' changes to 'i' in all stressed forms except nosotros/vosotros.
why_wrong: 'Me vesto' uses the wrong stem — 'vest-' must change to 'vist-' in the yo form.
'Me viste' uses the tú form — 'te vistes' = you get dressed; 'me visto' = I get dressed.
'Me vistío' is not a valid Spanish form.
questions.tip: Apply e→i to 'vest-'. The yo form ends in -o. Choose the correct reflexive pronoun for 'yo'.

questions.q: Which sentence correctly says 'I wake up at 7'?
questions.why_correct: 'Despertarse' (e→ie): yo = me despierto (stem 'despert-' → 'despiert-'). '¿A qué hora te despiertas?' = What time do you wake up?
why_wrong: 'Me desperto' forgets the e→ie stem change — must be 'despierto'.
'Se despierto' uses the wrong reflexive pronoun — 'se' is for él/ella, not yo.
'Me despierta' uses the él/ella ending (-a) — the yo form must end in -o.
questions.tip: Apply e→ie to 'despert-'. The yo form ends in -o. Which reflexive pronoun goes with 'yo'?

questions.why_correct: 'La boca' — 'bocadillo' (a Spanish sandwich) literally contains 'boca'. You eat a bocadillo with your mouth.
questions.tip: Think of 'bocadillo' — a popular Spanish snack. What body part does its name contain?

questions.why_correct: 'La boca' — found in 'bocadillo' (sandwich) and '¡Boca cerrada!' (Keep your mouth shut!).
questions.tip: Think of 'bocadillo' — a sandwich. What body part name does it contain?

questions.why_correct: 'La cabeza' shares a root with 'capital' (the head city of a country) and 'captain' (the head of a team).
questions.tip: Think of 'capital' — the leading city of a country. Both share a Latin root meaning this body part.

questions.why_correct: 'La cabeza' — related to 'capital' and 'cap' (a head covering). '¡Me duele la cabeza!' = My head hurts!
questions.tip: Think of 'cap' (a hat) or 'capital city' — both relate to the top or leading position.

questions.why_correct: 'El corazón' shares the Latin root 'cor' with English 'cordial' (warm-hearted) and 'core'.
questions.tip: Think of 'cordial' (warm and friendly) — its Latin root 'cor' points to a vital organ.

questions.why_correct: 'El corazón' — from Latin 'cor' (heart). 'Te quiero con todo mi corazón' = I love you with all my heart.
questions.tip: Think of 'cordial' — the Latin root 'cor' connects to this vital organ.

questions.why_correct: 'El dedo' — from Latin 'digitus', the same root as English 'digit'. Fingers and toes are digits.
questions.tip: Think of 'digit' — in math and anatomy, digits refer to individual units on the hands and feet.

questions.why_correct: 'El dedo' — from Latin 'digitus'. 'Dedo del pie' = toe; 'dedo de la mano' = finger.
questions.tip: Think of 'digit' — what are the individual units on your hands and feet called?

questions.why_correct: 'La espalda' is the part of your body that faces away. 'Me duele la espalda' = My back hurts.
questions.tip: Think of the part of your body that faces away when you turn around — the opposite of your chest.

questions.q: How do you say 'back (of the body)'?
questions.why_correct: 'La espalda' — the rear side of your torso. 'Me duele la espalda' = My back hurts.
questions.tip: Think of the body part opposite your chest — the side you can't see in a mirror.

questions.why_correct: 'El estómago' is a near-cognate of the English word. 'Me duele el estómago' = My stomach hurts.
questions.tip: This word looks and sounds very close to its English equivalent.

questions.why_correct: 'El estómago' — near-cognate of English 'stomach'. 'Tengo dolor de estómago' = I have a stomachache.
questions.tip: This word is a near-cognate — it looks almost identical to the English word.

questions.why_correct: 'El hombro' — the joint connecting your arm to your torso. 'Me encogí de hombros' = I shrugged.
questions.tip: Think of the joint at the top of your arm — what connects your arm to your body?

questions.why_correct: 'El hombro' — 'encogerse de hombros' = to shrug (literally 'to shrink the shoulders').
questions.tip: Think of the joint at the top of your arm — what body part do you shrug with?

questions.why_correct: 'La mano' shares Latin 'manus' with English 'manual' (done by hand) and 'manufacture' (made by hand).
questions.tip: Think of 'manual' (done by this body part) or 'manufacture' — same Latin root 'manus'.

questions.why_correct: 'La mano' — from Latin 'manus'. Note: despite ending in -o, it's feminine: 'la mano'. 'Dame la mano' = Give me your hand.
questions.tip: Think of 'manual' or 'manipulate' — from Latin 'manus', meaning this body part.

questions.why_correct: 'La nariz' — related to English 'nasal' (of the nose). 'Me sangra la nariz' = My nose is bleeding.
questions.tip: Think of 'nasal' — the adjective used to describe things relating to this facial feature.

questions.why_correct: 'La nariz' — from Latin 'naris'. Related to English 'nasal'. 'Tengo la nariz tapada' = My nose is stuffy.
questions.tip: Think of 'nasal' — what facial feature does that adjective describe?

questions.why_correct: 'La oreja' — from Latin 'auricula' (little ear), related to English 'auricular' (of the ear).
questions.tip: Think of 'auricular' — the adjective for things relating to this sense organ.

questions.why_correct: 'La oreja' — from Latin 'auricula'. 'Tengo los aretes en las orejas' = I have earrings in my ears.
questions.tip: Think of 'auricular' or 'audio' — from the Latin root for this sense organ.

questions.why_correct: 'El pecho' — related to 'pectoral' muscles, which are found in this area of the body.
questions.tip: Think of 'pectoral' muscles — what area of the body do they belong to?

questions.why_correct: 'El pecho' — from the same root as 'pectoral'. 'Me duele el pecho' = My chest hurts.

questions.why_correct: 'El pie' — from Latin 'pes/pedis', the same root as 'pedal', 'pedestrian', and 'pedicure'.
questions.tip: Think of 'pedal', 'pedestrian', or 'pedicure' — all from Latin 'pes/pedis'.

questions.why_correct: 'El pie' — from Latin 'pes/pedis'. 'Tengo frío en los pies' = My feet are cold.
questions.tip: Think of 'pedestrian' or 'pedicure' — from Latin 'pes/pedis', this body part.

questions.why_correct: 'La pierna' — the limb between your hip and your knee. 'Me rompí la pierna' = I broke my leg.
questions.tip: Think of the full limb that connects your hip to your foot — not the joint, the whole limb.

questions.why_correct: 'La pierna' — the full lower limb. 'Cruzar las piernas' = to cross your legs.
questions.tip: Think of the full limb you use to walk — from hip to foot, not just a joint.

questions.why_correct: 'La rodilla' — the joint in the middle of your leg. 'Arrodillarse' = to kneel (to put your rodilla on the ground).
questions.tip: Think of 'arrodillarse' (to kneel) — what body part touches the ground when you kneel?

questions.why_correct: 'La rodilla' — 'arrodillarse' = to kneel (to go down on your rodillas).
questions.tip: Think of 'arrodillarse' — the verb for kneeling. What body part lands on the ground?

questions.why_correct: 'El tobillo' — the joint connecting your foot to your leg. 'Me torcí el tobillo' = I twisted my ankle.
questions.tip: Think of the joint you twist when you step awkwardly — between the foot and the leg.

questions.why_correct: 'El tobillo' — 'Me torcí el tobillo' = I sprained my ankle.
questions.tip: Think of the joint between the foot and the leg — the one you sprain on uneven ground.

questions.q: What does 'la pasta de dientes' mean?
questions.why_correct: 'La pasta de dientes' — 'pasta' means paste, 'dientes' means teeth. The paste used on teeth.
questions.tip: Think of 'pasta' (paste) and 'dientes' (teeth) — what two-part bathroom product does this describe?

questions.why_correct: 'La pasta de dientes' — literally 'the paste of teeth'. Used with 'el cepillo de dientes'.
questions.tip: Think of 'pasta' (paste) + 'dientes' (teeth) — two words that together name this product.

questions.q: What does 'el cepillo de dientes' mean?
questions.why_correct: 'El cepillo de dientes' — 'cepillo' means brush, 'dientes' means teeth. The brush used on teeth.
questions.tip: Think of 'cepillo' (a brush) + 'dientes' (teeth) — what grooming tool does this describe?

questions.why_correct: 'El cepillo de dientes' — 'cepillo' = brush, 'dientes' = teeth. Used with 'cepillarse los dientes'.
why_wrong: 'La brocha de afeitar' means shaving brush.
questions.tip: Think of 'cepillo' (brush) + 'dientes' (teeth) — what tool is this?

questions.why_correct: 'El champú' is a near-cognate of English 'shampoo'. Used when 'ducharse' or 'bañarse'.
questions.tip: This word is a near-cognate — it looks and sounds very close to its English equivalent.

questions.why_correct: 'El champú' — near-cognate of English 'shampoo'. Used on the hair in the shower.

questions.why_correct: 'El acondicionador' is a near-cognate of English 'conditioner'. Used after el champú.
questions.tip: This near-cognate is used after shampoo — it looks very close to the English word.

questions.why_correct: 'El acondicionador' — near-cognate of 'conditioner'. Typically used after el champú.

questions.why_correct: 'El desodorante' is a near-cognate of 'deodorant'. 'Des-' = un-, 'odor' = smell.
questions.tip: Near-cognate — think of 'de-odor-ant'. The prefix 'des-' means un- or remove.

questions.why_correct: 'El desodorante' — near-cognate of 'deodorant'. 'Me pongo el desodorante' = I put on deodorant.
questions.tip: Near-cognate — 'des-' (un-) + 'odor' + '-ante'. What product removes body odor?

questions.why_correct: 'El jabón' — the bar or liquid you lather up with. Related to French 'savon' and Latin 'sapo'.
questions.tip: Think of the slippery bar or liquid you lather your body with in the shower.

questions.why_correct: 'El jabón' — 'Lávate las manos con jabón' = Wash your hands with soap.

questions.why_correct: 'La toalla' — the cloth you dry off with after 'ducharse' or 'bañarse'.
